title: Model Binding in ASP.NET Core — Beginner to Advanced
description: Learn how ASP.NET Core model binding works, from simple types to complex objects, collections, and file uploads.

data.text: What Is Model Binding?

Model binding is the automatic process that extracts data from an incoming HTTP request and maps it to action method parameters. Instead of manually reading form fields, query strings, or route values, you simply declare a parameter and ASP.NET Core populates it for you.

data.title: Why model binding matters
data.text: Model binding removes repetitive boilerplate code. Without it, you'd manually parse Request.Form, Request.Query, and RouteData.Values for every single field. Model binding does all of this automatically by matching names.

terms.definition: The ASP.NET Core feature that maps incoming HTTP request data to action method parameters.
A primitive C# type like int, string, bool, DateTime, or decimal.
A user-defined class whose public properties are individually bound from the request.
An attribute that tells model binding to look for a specific prefix on form field names.
An attribute that excludes a property from model binding, protecting it from over-posting.

data.text: Model Binding for Simple Types

When an action parameter is a simple type (int, string, bool, DateTime), model binding searches three sources in order: form data, then route values, then query strings. The first source with a matching key wins.

data.title: Default values for non-nullable types
data.text: If the parameter is a non-nullable int and no value is found, model binding applies the default value of 0. This can silently produce wrong results, so prefer nullable types (int?) with an explicit fallback.
Model Binding for Complex Types
When an action parameter is a complex type (a class), model binding binds each public writable property individually. It looks for keys named Property or Parent.Property for nested properties.

data.text: Using [Bind(Prefix)] for Non-Standard Form Names
When form field names do not match the model's property names, use [Bind(Prefix = "...")] to tell model binding which prefix to strip before matching properties.

data.title: Using [Bind(Prefix)] — Controller

data.text: Here, form fields named HomeAddress.City and HomeAddress.Country will bind to PersonAddress.City and PersonAddress.Country respectively. The Prefix value strips the "HomeAddress." part before matching.
Binding Selective Properties with [Bind] and [BindNever]

The [Bind] attribute can whitelist specific properties. Any property not listed is excluded from binding — a security technique to prevent over-posting. The [BindNever] attribute does the same thing but is applied directly on the model property.

data.title: Using [Bind] to Whitelist Properties — Controller
Using [BindNever] to Exclude a Property — Model
Prevent over-posting with BindNever
data.text: Over-posting occurs when a malicious user sends extra form fields to set properties you did not intend to expose. Applying [BindNever] to sensitive properties like IsAdmin or Salary on your model is a critical security practice.
Model Binding for Collections
Model binding supports arrays and lists. When multiple form fields share the same name, ASP.NET Core automatically creates an array or List<T> from their values.

data.title: Binding a String Array from Repeated Form Fields
Razor View with Repeated Input Names for Array Binding

data.text: All three inputs have name="places". On submission, model binding collects all values with that name into a string array and passes it to the Places action.
Model Binding for Collections of Complex Types
To bind a collection of complex types, use indexed field names like [0].City, [1].City. The index in square brackets tells model binding which list item each field belongs to.

data.text: Model Binding for File Uploads
Model binding also handles file uploads. When a form includes a file input with enctype="multipart/form-data", the uploaded file is bound to an IFormFile parameter.

data.title: Three things required for file upload binding
items: Add an <input type="file" name="file" /> control in the view.
Add an IFormFile parameter to the action method — model binding fills it automatically.

data.text: Exercise: Build a Contact Form

data.title: Contact Form with Nested Address Binding
data.description: Create a ContactViewModel with Name, Email, and a nested Address object (Street, City, Country). Build a Razor form that posts to an action and model-binds the full object.
steps: Create ContactViewModel with Name (string), Email (string), and Address (class with Street, City, Country).
Create a GET action that returns the empty form.
Create a POST action that accepts ContactViewModel and checks ModelState.IsValid.
Build the Razor form using asp-for tag helpers for all fields including nested address fields.
Submit the form and verify all properties are bound correctly.
data.expectedOutcome: All form fields are correctly bound to the ContactViewModel, including nested Address properties. Inspect the model in the POST action to confirm values.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Model binding automatically maps request data to action method parameters.
Simple types are bound from form data, then route values, then query strings.
Complex types have each public property bound individually from form field names.
Nested objects use dot notation: HomeAddress.City maps to Address.City.
Use [Bind(Prefix)] when form field names have a non-matching prefix.
Use [BindNever] on model properties to prevent over-posting attacks.
Collections bind from repeated field names (arrays) or indexed names (lists of complex types).
File uploads use IFormFile with enctype="multipart/form-data" on the form.
data.takeaway: Model binding is the bridge between HTTP requests and your C# action methods. Mastering it is essential for every ASP.NET Core developer.
